newsitem.title: FRANCE: French planters have no plans for new ETBE plants.
newsitem.headline: French planters have no plans for new ETBE plants.

text.p: French sugar beet planters said on Thursday it would be too costly to participate in the construction of new ETBE (Ethyl-Tertio-Butyl-Ether) plants in France to meet future demand for crop-based oil additives or bio-fuels.
They were instead considering using two existing plants that petrochemical group ARCO planned to convert from MTBE (Methyl-Tertiary-Butyl-Ether) to ETBE production.
ARCO owns two plants producing MTBE, made from natural-gas based methanol, one in Fos in southern France and another in Rotterdam.
ETBE is produced from sugar beet and wheat-based ethanol combined with isobutane.
"We had contacts with ARCO. If they start producing ETBE, we would act as suppliers," the president of the CGB planters federation Dominique Ducroquet told a news conference.
Ducroquet said it was too costly for planters to directly invest in the construction of new plants.
The French parliament recently approved a draft law on clean air that makes the use of oxygenated components in fuel mandatory by 2000.

French grain and beet growers have long advocated mandatory use of oil additives grown on set-aside land as they offer a promising outlet for farm production curtailed under the reform of the European Union's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).
The government has yet to decide on the percentage of oxygenated components that will be made mandatory in fuel.
Assuming two percent, beet-based ethanol production would eventually jump to 8.8 million hectolitres from a 1996 level of 730,000 and an estimated 1997 level of 812,000, planters said.
This would be equivalent to 55,000 hectares of beet against 10,580 in 1996 and 11,800 in 1997.

Elf Aquitaine produces ETBE at its Feysin plant. Sugar beet planters, grain and sugar industry groups and Total are producing ETBE at Gonfreville and Dunkirk. The three plants will reach full capacity in 1997, planters said.
